blocks.text: The chapter’s images of bearing sin, wounds and healing, and sheep that wander combine scriptural and pastoral language. They are central to the passage’s account of how the servant’s suffering benefits others, but they do not by themselves settle the form of later atonement theories.

Mark 10:45 later links the Son of Man’s service and death with a ransom “for many,” echoing the language of Isaiah 53:11–12. How that connection should be understood—through liberation, the servant, martyrdom, covenant, or atonement—remains debated.

Isaiah 52:13–53:12 tells of a servant’s humiliation, suffering, death, representative bearing, vindication, and benefit to others, yet it never explicitly names the servant. Collective, individual, prophetic, messianic, and Christian readings therefore have long histories. It is important to distinguish the passage’s literary sense and possible historical referent from later claims of prediction, typology, quotation, or broader canonical interpretation. The Old Greek translation of Isaiah is itself an ancient Jewish interpretation: some differences may reflect a different underlying Hebrew text, while others may reflect the translator’s choices. The Great Isaiah Scroll and other Qumran manuscripts also show that Isaiah was actively transmitted and interpreted.

sections.title: The servant in Isaiah and later reading
